summaries.summary: Relation classification assigns sentences with two marked entities to predefined relations, with early classifiers recently outperformed by NNs on SemEval 2010 shared task 8 data.
This study investigates RNNs, CNNs, and their combination, and lists contributions.
The authors propose extended middle context, a CNN context representation using all sentence parts and emphasizing the middle part.
The authors present connectionist bi-directional RNN models combining intermediate hidden layers and introduce ranking loss for RNN optimization in relation classification.
CNNs and RNNs are combined using a simple voting scheme and achieve new state-of-the-art results on the SemEval 2010 benchmark dataset.
In 2010, manually annotated relation classification data was released for a SemEval shared task, where NNs later outperformed support vector machines and maximum entropy classifiers.
Prior CNN work used middle context, lexical features, multiple filter sizes, and ranking layers, with deSantos2015 publishing the best SemEval result so far.
socher used recursive neural networks with syntactic parsing, while zhang investigated a bi-directional temporal structured RNN with words and a pooling layer.
CNNs convolve sentence word embeddings with filters, apply max-pooling, concatenate values, and classify the expressed relation.
Extended middle context splits contexts into left, middle, and right regions, repeats the middle context in two CNN inputs, and concatenates pooled results.
The convolutional layer uses 2D filters spanning all embedding dimensions, max pooling, and multi-windows with window sizes 2-5.
The RNN models whole sentences before predicting output, uses backpropagation through time, and applies gradient clipping with a threshold of 10.
Initial experiments showed trigrams as input were superior, so each timestep concatenates corresponding word embeddings into a trigram.
Bi-directional RNNs use both a history vector and a future vector because succeeding words may help process relation arguments.
The network has a forward pass, a backward pass, and a combination of both, all trained jointly.
The connectionist bi-directional RNN adds a connection to the previous combined hidden layer to include all intermediate hidden layers in the final decision.
Experiments compare this RNN with uni-directional RNNs and bi-directional RNNs without additional hidden layer connections.
Words are represented by concatenated vectors consisting of a word embedding and a position feature vector.
word2vec trained embeddings on an English Wikipedia from May 2014, considering words appearing more than 100 times and adding a PADDING token.
Randomly initialized position embeddings are incorporated, and RNN experiments investigate position embeddings, entity presence flags, and position indicators.
The ranking loss function from deSantos2015 maximizes the distance between the true label and the best competitive label for a data point.
The ranking objective uses class scores, penalization, margins, deSantos2015 settings, and no learned pattern for class Other.
The SemEval 2010 task 8 dataset has 19 relations, 8,000 training sentences, 2,717 test sentences, and macro F1 evaluation.
RNN and CNN models used theano, L2 regularization with weight 0.0001, specified training settings, and a 6.5k/1.5k training/development split.
The authors also report ensemble results combining the presented single models with a voting process.
A zeng2014-like CNN baseline using middle context and 1200 filters obtains 73.0, improving to 78.6 with 5 dimensional position features.
CNN experiments add multi-windows, ranking layer, extended middle context, and larger embeddings, with ranking layer and embedding size especially impacting performance.
A uni-directional RNN baseline predicting after processing the whole sentence achieves an F1 score of 61.2 on the SemEval test set.
Position indicators perform best on SemEval data with an F1 score of 73.4, though not significantly better than position embeddings with entity flags.
RNN models are varied by bi-directionality, hidden layer connections, ranking instead of softmax, and word embedding dimension 400.
All RNN variations in Table TABREF14 yield statistically significant improvements, especially hidden layer connections and the ranking layer.
Voting over several CNN and RNN models achieves an F1 score of 84.9, supporting complementary information from RNNs and CNNs.
ER-CNN and R-RNN obtain state-of-the-art results on SemEval 2010 task 8 without using any linguistic features.
The paper investigated CNN and RNN features and architectures without linguistic features, introduced new representations and ranking RNNs, and achieved state-of-the-art SemEval 2010 task 8 results.
Heike Adel receives the Google European Doctoral Fellowship in Natural Language Processing, which supports this research.
This research was also supported by Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft grant SCHU 2246/4-2.
